title: Tata Sons Leadership Battle Intensifies as Chandrasekaran's Future Hangs in Balance
excerpt: A power struggle between Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata and Tata Sons chairman N. Chandrasekaran is drawing comparisons to the Cyrus Mistry ouster, with a crucial AGM days away.
body:
• Tata Sons chairman N. Chandrasekaran has reportedly discussed stepping down ahead of the August 18 AGM amid unresolved tensions with Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata over succession, performance and the listing question.
  • Noel Tata, who controls the charitable trusts that own nearly two-thirds of Tata Sons, has emerged as the decisive power broker in both the leadership succession and the debate over whether the $277 billion conglomerate should go public.
  • The board deferred Chandrasekaran's reappointment in February after Noel raised concerns about losses at Air India, Tata Digital and other new ventures, along with unresolved questions about a potential IPO.
  • The standoff echoes the 2016 removal of Cyrus Mistry, raising fresh concerns about governance stability at India's oldest and largest conglomerate.

The power struggle at Tata Sons between chairman N. Chandrasekaran and Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata has intensified ahead of an August 18 annual general meeting, with reports suggesting Chandrasekaran has discussed the possibility of stepping down amid uncertainty over his reappointment.

The Economic Times reported on August 12 that Chandrasekaran had discussed a potential departure with people close to the situation, citing tensions with Noel Tata that have made his position increasingly untenable. Reuters Breakingviews described the row as centering on whether to list the holding company Chandrasekaran has led for nine years.

Noel Tata's Rise to Power

For decades, Noel Tata built retail and trading businesses out of the spotlight that followed his half-brother Ratan Tata. Now, as chairman of the philanthropic trusts that together own about 66% of Tata Sons — including the Sir Ratan Tata Trust and Sir Dorabji Tata Trust with a combined 52% stake — he occupies one of the most powerful positions in Indian corporate governance.

Noel, 68, emerged as a central figure after Ratan Tata's death in October 2024. Trustees unanimously appointed him chairman of Tata Trusts, and he subsequently joined the Tata Sons board as a non-executive director.

"The job is to find the most effective allocation of the resources we have, make choices on how to deploy those resources meaningfully, and do what is best for India."

— Noel Tata, speaking at an event this month, as reported by Reuters

His influence over Tata Sons' succession process and role in the listing debate could shape the future of one of India's best-known conglomerates, with a combined market value of around $277 billion, according to Reuters.

The February Boardroom Showdown

The current tensions trace back to a February 25 board meeting at Bombay House that was expected to formalize a third term for Chandrasekaran. Instead, Noel led discussions that exposed deep disagreements.

According to The Hindu BusinessLine, Noel raised the issue of underperformance at several group entities, including Air India, as well as Chandrasekaran's handling of events following the London-bound flight crash. He also questioned continuing losses at Tata Digital, Infiniti Retail and Tata Neu.

A separate concern centered on Tata Sons' potential public listing. The Reserve Bank of India classified Tata Sons as an "upper-layer" non-banking financial company in 2022, potentially requiring it to go public within three years. Chandrasekaran reportedly told the board he favored keeping Tata Sons private but could not guarantee an RBI exemption, according to Business Standard reporting cited by Dhanamon.

"I recommended that it should be deferred, because of request from some directors," Chandrasekaran told media while leaving Bombay House after the meeting, declining to elaborate further.

Competing Visions for Tata Sons

Noel has pushed for a new leadership structure at Tata Sons with separate roles for chairman, CEO and managing director, and deputy CEO, Mint reported. He favored a truncated two-year extension for Chandrasekaran — rather than the usual five — to allow time to institute a succession process.

Not all trustees agree. TVS Motor chairman emeritus Venu Srinivasan and retired defence secretary Vijay Singh have backed a full third five-year term for Chandrasekaran, according to Mint.

The financial case for Chandrasekaran is significant. From FY18 to FY25, Tata Sons' consolidated revenue tripled and net profit more than tripled. He oversaw the group's entry into aviation, iPhone assembly and e-commerce. But Noel's concern about the capital commitments — over $11 billion invested in Air India, Tata Electronics and Tata Digital — and surging losses has created a fundamental tension over strategic direction.

The Mistry Parallel

The standoff has inevitably drawn comparisons to the 2016 removal of Cyrus Mistry, Ratan Tata's chosen successor who was ousted after barely four years as chairman. Mistry's removal triggered one of India's biggest corporate governance battles, with court proceedings dragging on for years.

Noel is Mistry's brother-in-law, adding a personal dimension to the current power dynamics. Multiple sources told BusinessLine that events at the February board meeting showed "an increasingly assertive Noel Tata, who has been consolidating his hold over the group by quietly getting rid of the opposition."

Noel's son Neville Tata and his confidant Bhaskar Bhat have joined the Sir Dorab Tata Trust board, while departures of former trustees including businessman Mehli Mistry and former Citibank CEO Pramit Jhaveri have reshaped the trust's leadership composition.

What's Next

The August 18 AGM looms as a potential flashpoint. Without a fresh term, Chandrasekaran's leadership of India's largest conglomerate ends in February 2027. Whether the meeting produces a resolution — or deepens the impasse — will signal whether Tata Sons can navigate its latest leadership crisis without the governance turmoil that has marred its recent history.
nri_angle: The leadership battle at India's largest conglomerate directly affects Tata group stocks widely held by NRI investors globally.
